nodes.title: Revisions
nodes.body:
Jan 1, 1994.  TD Phillips

note: There was no date on the original document so 1994 Jan 1 was assigned since most of the SLHs were prepared from 1994 thru 1997.

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name:  southern kingfish
Scientific Name: Menticirrhus americanus

nodes.title: CLASSIFICATION
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
      Class: Osteichthys
      Order: Perciformes
      Family : Sciaenidae

Other Common Names:  whiting (312 664), kingfish, roundhead, sea mink, king whiting (312 834), sea mullet (312 327 834) , Virginia mullet, Carolina whiting (834).

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Historically fished in the Chesapeake and off North Carolina, but did not comprise an important fishery (312 834). Caught in bottom trawls, seines, and gillnets (312 791). Commercial landings in Florida in 1982 were less than 1.0 million pounds worth about $367,000 dockside value (902). Average size in northern markets ranges from 0.5 to 2.5 pounds (312).
Recreational: Caught on hook and line particularly in the surf along beaches (312 791). Commonly caught by fishermen in the Tampa Bay area (664). Considered to be a good quality food fish (312 834).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  New York to Texas and the Bay of Campeche to Argentina (312 327 363 788). Common south of Chesapeake Bay ( 3 1 2 ) . Rare or absent in south Florida and the Antilles (788).
Within Study Area: Found throughout Florida waters, with the exception of extreme South Florida (312 327 788).

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body: Primarily a bottom species which are often found in schools; the young are found in schools along the beaches (664 832 1021).

nodes.title: Movements/Migrations
nodes.body: Larvae may be transported far up tidal rivers, then actively move to higher salinity waters as they grow (1045). Adults migrate into sounds and tidal rivers in the fall after spawning in South Carolina (1045). Reported to move offshore to deeper waters in cold weather, particularly in temperate regions (252 303 1045).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type: Found in shallow coastal waters and common along the beaches (664 788). Taken in nearshore waters out to a depth of about 67 m (363 833). Also inhabits estuarine waters, moving into sounds and tidal rivers (664 1045).
Substrate: Frequently found on open sandy beaches (312 664 1045). Found over mud, sand, mud-sand mixtures, and mud-shell mixtures (1045). Prefer clear sandy bottoms along beaches and near mouths of coastal sounds (1045).

nodes.title: Eggs/Larvae
nodes.body: Juvenile/adults: Taken at temperatures as low as 60 C. (1045), but also as high as 32.50 C. (224). Springer and Woodburn (664) reported juveniles and adults from Tampa Bay at temperatures ranging from 12.5 to 310 C. At Cedar Key, Reid (581) collected specimens at temperatures from 10.0 to 27-10 C., and in Texas, specimens were collected at temperatures from 13.7 to 30.50 C. (255).

nodes.title: Eggs/Larvae
nodes.body: Juvenile/adults: Taken at salinities from 1.9 to 41.0 %, but most common above 24 to 30 % (312 1046). Specimens have been collected at salinities from 13.7 to 35.1 % in Tampa Bay (6641, from 17.5 to 25.5 % at Cedar Key (581), and from 14.4 to 36.7 % in Texas (255).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode: Sexual reproduction; broadcast spawner with pelagic eggs.
Fecundity: Males mature at about age II and a size of about 195 mm; females mature at age I1 or III at a size of 230-250 mm (1045). Spawning occurs primarily offshore (832 1045 1046). Springer and Woodburn (664) suggested that spawning occurs from May-June in the Tampa Bay area based on the presence of young. At Cedar Key, ripe females were collected in April and August (581). Females with well developed roe have been taken from April through June along the Louisiana coast (252). All specimens examined from March and April from Aransas Bay, Texas were ripe (467). Hildebrand and Cable (832) reported an April through August or September spawning season in North Carolina. Ripe and spent females were collected during May and June in the Chesapeake Bay (312). Springer and Woodburn (664) speculated that spawning takes place at about the same time of year throughout the range of the species.

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Eggs/Larvae: No information on egg development available.
Larvae: stages range from 1.5 to 7.0 mm (363 832 1047).
Juveniles/Adults: Juveniles attain the full adult fin ray complement by 5-8 mm (832 1047). Individuals as small as 25 mrn in July may reach 117 mm by October in the Tampa Bay area (664). Reported to reach 40 mm by their first winter in New Jersey, about 160 rnm by the second winter, and 250 mm by the third winter (312). Average length by the end of the first summer at Beaufort, NC is reported as 116 mm and averages 135 mm by November (832). In South Carolina, reported to reach 150-160 mm by the second summer, and 220-230 mm by the third summer (1045). Maximum size recorded is 419 mm and 1.1 kg (312).

nodes.title: Trophic Modes
nodes.body: Primarily a bottom feeder (664). In Chesapeake Bay, the diet consists of 85% crustaceans (primarily shrimp), and 15% fish (312 832). Smith (834) reported molluscs, fish, and crustaceans in the stomachs of fish collected in North Carolina. Fishes collected in Texas waters contained several species of crabs, fish, and shrimp with shrimp accounting for the largest proportion of the stomach contents (467). In the Tampa Bay area, Springer and Woodburn (664) found polychaetes, crabs, mysids, Emerita, and unidentifiable remains. Similar food items were found in fish taken at Cedar Key (581).
